cim: SBA pushes to enact printing initiative before finals, implement new artificial intelligence exam guidelines
cim_eredeti: SBA pushes to enact printing initiative before finals, implement new artificial intelligence exam guidelines
szoveg_eredeti:
The Student Bar Association passed a resolution urging GW Law to develop alternative guidelines surrounding the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms that would still allow students to utilize online materials and not solely rely on printed resources at the body’s last meeting of the semester Tuesday.

SBA senators unanimously approved the Combatting Technology Resource Limitations Fairly, or “Ctrl+F,” Resolution which calls upon law officials and faculty to address the risk of students committing AI-related academic misconduct through enacting “stronger preventative procedures” — like changing exam software to one that can better detect AI assistance — rather than prohibiting students from using any computer-downloaded material at all. Senators said due to professors’ fear of AI use on exams, students have had to print more materials this semester, causing some students to run out of the $30 of printing credit the University allots each student for the academic year.

Some professors nationwide have implemented technology bans or reverted to paper exams and textbooks in response to an increase of AI-related academic misconduct cases. In April, Conflict Education & Student Accountability reported a 47 percent increase in academic misconduct cases at the University overall from spring 2023 to 2025, saying AI usage fueled the increase.

SBA Sen. Michael Distler said students can access textbooks downloaded to their computers in open-hard-drive exams, however the ability to download an AI-agent to a computer hard drive has dissuaded professors from using the open-hard-drive model. He said many professors now opt to use a closed-hard-drive format, which means a student cannot have an AI-agent take the exam in their place, but also cannot access downloaded textbooks during exams.

Distler said the University should look into replacing its exam software so students could still access their hard-drives to use downloaded textbooks during exams, but would be caught if they tried to employ AI assistance.

“They need to look into a new exam software that is capable of dealing with this, and I’m sure that exists because anybody in academia is worried about this and trying to address it,” Distler said.

SBA senators Nathaniel Rutledge and Jack Korologos then introduced the Ctrl+F resolution, which asks the law school to investigate solutions and provide findings, which SBA committees would report to the Senate, by the end of next semester to address AI misconduct. The resolution states the current solution of reducing AI usage by increasing students’ reliance on printed materials imposes printing costs and a “logistical hardship” on students, adding that the “burden” would fall hardest on students facing financial hardship.

“This wouldn’t be barking at professors who already have that closed book, open note setup, or some sort of process,” Korologos said. “It’s really against the University administration at large. That’s where we’re focused.”

The SBA allocated $38,249 of the body’s funds to a new printing initiative — created at the recommendation of GW Law Dean Dayna Bowen Matthew — in September to increase the $30 printing credit each law student receives at the start of each academic year to $52, though SBA President Juliana Fernandez said in her presidential report the funds have not yet been transferred to student accounts. She said Matthew and Senior Associate Dean for Academic Affairs Laurie S. Kohn told her in a meeting last month they aim to transfer the funds to students by Dec. 1, but it could be delayed to Jan. 1 given the “amount of coordination” required, including gathering students’ GW IDs and email addresses, coordinating with GW Information Technology and setting up invoicing information.

SBA Sen. Ethan Briggs, a senator for the 1L Robert Jackson Inn, said he and some of his constituents ran out of their annual printing funds last month because they needed to print out an entire textbook and notes for a course that prohibits computer use. He said he has already spent an additional $15 out of pocket on printing this semester after exhausting the University’s printing credit.

“I just want to stress how important this is to me, and to future 1L classes,” Briggs said. “We should not be paying our own money on top of tuition in order to bring required materials.”

Fernandez, who said she has another meeting with Matthew and Kohn on Thursday, said she plans to emphasize to officials the urgency of having additional printing credits in students’ accounts by Dec. 1, which would fall before finals when students likely need to print additional material for exams.

SBA Sen. Lauren Bernard also said the SBA should ask law officials if they could budget to permanently provide law students with additional printing credits as opposed to having the SBA allocate funds from their account to increase students’ printing funds, which they did at the start of the semester.

While Fernandez confirmed at the meeting that non-graduating law students’ unused printing credits will roll over to the next academic year, Bernard said the SBA should also advocate that graduating law students’ unused funds be put into a “printing pool” to ensure the funds are turned into printing credit for other students.

“It alleviates the amount of money that the administration has to set aside to give to us every year, which is not guaranteed,” Bernard said. “They’re not guaranteed this extra $20 next year.”

The SBA allocated over $300,000 towards its executive budget and law student organizations this September, almost double the amount the University gave the SBA for their budget the year before.

Senators allocated $475 of the ad hoc budget to a law student to reimburse his travel expenses for attending a conference in Mexico. The ad hoc budget now stands at $17,637.

Senators also elected Bernard to serve as trial speaker of the senate for next semester.

Law students ratified the body’s constitutional amendment to create a speaker of the senate role — who will take on the executive vice president’s role of presiding over the Senate to allow the vice president to work more closely with the executive branch — during October elections. While the amendment officially goes into effect next fall, senators will have a trial period in the spring to test out the new role and pass any amendments as needed.

The SBA has not yet released a date for its first Senate meeting of the next semester.
